where: Section 1 formula, Section 3 table (Sensitivity), worked example 1 and exam traps
problem: The same symbol K carries two different units in one chapter. The formula V_out = K·x defines K in volts per millimetre, and the worked example uses K = 0.50 V/mm at 5 V rms excitation, so the arithmetic 0.40/0.50 = 0.80 mm only works in V/mm. The table instead defines sensitivity as 'output per millimetre per volt of excitation, in mV/(mm·V)', and the last exam trap says sensitivity is quoted per volt of excitation. A student who takes the table definition and plugs a datasheet figure of, say, 100 mV/(mm·V) straight into x = V_out/K will be wrong by the excitation voltage.
fix: Keep one definition and link the two. Say: 'Sensitivity is sometimes quoted per volt of excitation, S in mV/(mm·V); at an excitation of V_exc volts rms the constant in V_out = K·x is K = S × V_exc, in volts per millimetre.' Then state in worked example 1 that K = 0.50 V/mm applies at the 5 V rms excitation given, and in the trap say 'sensitivity per volt of excitation must be multiplied by the actual drive voltage before it is used as K'.

problem: LVDT is never expanded at first use. The full name appears only in the last line of the 'Beyond' note, so a student meeting the abbreviation in the title and lead has to guess it.
fix: Open with: 'An LVDT (linear variable differential transformer) turns a small straight-line movement of a magnetic core into an AC voltage.'

problem: The reason given does not match the property. Resolution is set by the readout electronics because there is no sliding contact to cause stiction or wear; 'because the core never rubs on the former' explains the absence of friction, not the link to the electronics.
fix: Write: 'Set by the readout electronics, not by the winding, because the core has no sliding contact, so there is no stiction and the output changes continuously with position.'
